source_refs.note: Book p. 284: 14.4.2 volume of the parallelepiped as (u x v).w, base area and height, the three cyclic forms, with its figure. Book errors: modulus bar missing in (i); 'be taking'. Teaching notes, Key points, mistakes are ours.

blocks.text: The triple scalar product \((\underline{u}\times \underline{v})\cdot \underline{w}\) represents the volume of the parallelepiped having \(\underline{u}\), \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{w}\) as its conterminous edges.

blocks.alt: A flat parallelepiped on three vectors u, v, w from the corner O. The base spanned by u and v is hatched and labelled Area of base = |u x v|. The vector u x v rises vertically from O; the angle theta lies between it and w. A dashed line from the tip of w meets the vertical at M with a right angle; a bar on the left marks height = |w| cos theta.
blocks.caption: Figure: parallelepiped with edges u, v, w; base area |u × v|, height |w| cos θ (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A parallelepiped is a "slanted box": a solid with six faces, each face a parallelogram, opposite faces equal and parallel. A brick or a matchbox is the special case in which every face is a rectangle.
Conterminous edges are edges that start from the same corner. Here \(\underline{u}\), \(\underline{v}\), \(\underline{w}\) all start at the corner \(O\); the other nine edges are copies of these three.
As it is seen from the formula that:

blocks.text_alt: (u cross v) dot w equals modulus of u cross v times modulus of w times cos theta

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: This is the definition of the dot product, \(\underline{a}\cdot \underline{b} = |\underline{a}||\underline{b}|\cos\theta\), with \(\underline{a} = \underline{u}\times \underline{v}\) and \(\underline{b} = \underline{w}\). So \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\underline{w}\) and the vector \(\underline{u}\times \underline{v}\), which stands perpendicular to the base (see the figure), not the angle between \(\underline{w}\) and the base.

items: (i) \(|\underline{u}\times \underline{v}\) = area of the parallelogram with two adjacent sides \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In (i) the book prints "|u × v =" without the closing bar of the modulus. It should read \(|\underline{u}\times \underline{v}|\) = area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is \(|\underline{w}|\cos\theta\) the height? The height is measured straight up from the base, that is along \(\underline{u}\times \underline{v}\). In the figure, the dashed line from the tip of \(\underline{w}\) meets that vertical line at \(M\) at a right angle, so the triangle formed by \(O\), \(M\) and the tip of \(\underline{w}\) is right-angled at \(M\). Its hypotenuse is \(|\underline{w}|\) and the angle at \(O\) is \(\theta\), so
\[OM = |\underline{w}|\cos\theta\]
(adjacent side = hypotenuse \(\times\cos\theta\)). \(OM\) is exactly the height of the top face above the base.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: This is the familiar rule "volume = area of base \(\times\) height", the same rule you use for a box or a cylinder. The scalar triple product just does both jobs at once: \(|\underline{u}\times \underline{v}|\) gives the base and \(|\underline{w}|\cos\theta\) gives the height.

Similarly, be taking the base plane formed by \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{w}\), we have
\[\text{Volume} = (\underline{v}\times \underline{w})\cdot \underline{u}\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "be taking the base plane". It should read "by taking the base plane".

And by taking the base plane formed by \(\underline{w}\) and \(\underline{u}\), we have
\[\text{Volume} = (\underline{w}\times \underline{u})\cdot \underline{v}\]

blocks.text_alt: (u cross v) dot w equals (v cross w) dot u equals (w cross u) dot v

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The same box can stand on any of its three different pairs of faces; its volume does not change. That is why the three cyclic forms are equal. Since the dot product is commutative, \((\underline{v}\times \underline{w})\cdot \underline{u} = \underline{u}\cdot(\underline{v}\times \underline{w})\), so this also shows
\[(\underline{u}\times \underline{v})\cdot \underline{w} = \underline{u}\cdot(\underline{v}\times \underline{w})\]
the dot and the cross can change places (Example 23 proves the same with determinants).
A sign warning: if \(\underline{w}\) points to the other side of the base from \(\underline{u}\times \underline{v}\), then \(\theta > 90^{\circ}\), \(\cos\theta < 0\) and the product is negative. The volume is then the absolute value of the product (see the Note in 14.4.3).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Quick check with a brick: \(\underline{u} = 2\underline{i}\), \(\underline{v} = 3\underline{j}\), \(\underline{w} = 4\underline{k}\) form a \(2\times 3\times 4\) box. Then \(\underline{u}\times \underline{v} = 6\underline{k}\) and \((\underline{u}\times \underline{v})\cdot \underline{w} = 6\underline{k}\cdot 4\underline{k} = 24 = 2\cdot 3\cdot 4\), the volume you expect.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Volume of the parallelepiped with conterminous edges \(\underline{u}, \underline{v}, \underline{w}\) is \((\underline{u}\times \underline{v})\cdot \underline{w}\) (taken as a positive number).
2. \(|\underline{u}\times \underline{v}|\) = area of the base; \(|\underline{w}|\cos\theta\) = height, \(\theta\) being the angle between \(\underline{w}\) and \(\underline{u}\times \underline{v}\).
3. \((\underline{u}\times \underline{v})\cdot \underline{w} = (\underline{v}\times \underline{w})\cdot \underline{u} = (\underline{w}\times \underline{u})\cdot \underline{v}\).
4. Dot and cross can be interchanged: \((\underline{u}\times \underline{v})\cdot \underline{w} = \underline{u}\cdot(\underline{v}\times \underline{w})\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Taking \(\theta\) as the angle between \(\underline{w}\) and the base; it is the angle between \(\underline{w}\) and the perpendicular \(\underline{u}\times \underline{v}\).
2. Using \(|\underline{w}|\) as the height: the height is \(|\underline{w}|\cos\theta\), which is smaller unless \(\underline{w}\) is perpendicular to the base.
3. Giving a negative volume: a volume is always the absolute value of the triple product.
